raw_text:
Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were introduced to extend the benefits of drug-eluting stents while avoiding a permanent metallic cage. The theoretical advantages—late restoration of vasomotion, adaptive remodelling, facilitation of future bypass grafting or reintervention, and reduced very-late neoatherosclerosis—were compelling. Early first-in-human ABSORB studies with the poly-L-lactic acid everolimus-eluting scaffold showed acceptable short-term safety, serial imaging evidence of strut coverage and bioresorption, and signals of vasomotor recovery [1-4]. These mechanistic observations generated enthusiasm that “vascular restorative therapy” might transform percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI).

Randomised evidence, however, reshaped the field. ABSORB II initially suggested broadly comparable 1-year clinical outcomes but later failed its co-primary vasomotion and late-lumen-loss endpoints, with excess target-vessel myocardial infarction and scaffold thrombosis at 3 years [5,6]. ABSORB III met non-inferiority for 1-year target-lesion failure in relatively simple lesions, but subsequent follow-up and ABSORB IV demonstrated that early safety remained vulnerable, especially when small vessels, suboptimal expansion or inadequate post-dilatation were present [7,8]. Regional trials in China and Japan showed acceptable 1-year angiographic and clinical performance in carefully selected lesions [9,10], whereas STEMI-focused TROFI II suggested favourable healing at 6 months but was underpowered for rare safety endpoints [11]. EVERBIO II, a pragmatic single-centre study, reinforced that angiographic efficacy was not clearly superior to contemporary drug-eluting stents (DES) [12].

The most sobering evidence came from broader practice. In the AIDA all-comers trial, the Absorb scaffold did not reduce target-vessel failure and was associated with significantly more device thrombosis than everolimus-eluting metallic stents [13]. Pooled analyses and meta-analyses consistently confirmed an excess of scaffold thrombosis and target-lesion events with first-generation Absorb BVS, particularly during the first 3 years, the period of active bioresorption [14-18]. These findings led to withdrawal or restriction of the Absorb platform and a major reassessment of patient selection, device design and implantation technique.

Several lessons are now clear. First, BVS are not simply “dissolving stents”; their mechanical constraints matter. Thick struts increase flow disturbance, platelet activation and side-branch compromise, while polymeric scaffolds have limited overexpansion capacity and are susceptible to recoil, fracture and late dismantling if malapposed. Second, implantation technique is central. Contemporary recommendations emphasised the “PSP” concept—proper lesion preparation, accurate sizing and high-pressure post-dilatation—often aided by intravascular imaging [19-21]. Third, any potential late benefit of leaving no implant is clinically irrelevant unless early and mid-term safety matches best-in-class DES.

The field has therefore shifted toward thinner-strut and faster-resorbing platforms. Magnesium-based scaffolds are attractive because they behave more like metallic stents during deployment and resorb faster than poly-L-lactic acid devices. BIOSOLVE-I and BIOSOLVE-II established early feasibility of drug-eluting absorbable magnesium scaffolds, and longer-term BIOSOLVE-II follow-up suggested sustained safety in selected de novo lesions [22-25]. The larger BIOSOLVE-IV registry reported low scaffold-thrombosis rates when the Magmaris scaffold was used according to instructions and with careful technique [26]. However, the MAGSTEMI randomised trial cautioned that magnesium scaffolds in STEMI may increase angiographic late lumen loss compared with permanent sirolimus-eluting stents, although clinical event rates were low and longer follow-up remained informative [27,28]. Third-generation DREAMS 3G/BIOMAG-I data are encouraging, with improved radial strength, thinner struts and low 12-month event rates, but randomised comparisons with contemporary DES are still needed [29,30].

At present, routine BVS use in PCI cannot be recommended outside trials or carefully controlled registries. Contemporary ultrathin-strut DES remain the benchmark for safety, deliverability and efficacy. Future BVS must demonstrate DES-like acute performance, broad vessel-size applicability, low thrombogenicity, predictable resorption, and superiority—or at least non-inferiority with a credible late advantage—in adequately powered randomised trials. The concept remains biologically appealing, but the Absorb experience established that “leaving nothing behind” is valuable only if nothing is left behind safely.
